subject: physics
title: Properties of electromagnetic waves 1
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Properties of electromagnetic waves 1 — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.6.2.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Properties of electromagnetic waves 1, specification section 4.6.2.2.
final_note: You worked through Properties of electromagnetic waves 1 — 7 specification statements.

concepts.def: When a wave meets a substance and its energy is transferred into that substance rather than continuing through it. The wave does not emerge on the far side, and the internal energy of the substance rises.
When a wave passes through a substance and continues on the other side of it. A substance that transmits a wave allows it through with little of its energy being absorbed.
When a wave meets a boundary and is sent back into the substance it came from, instead of passing into the second substance.

The change in direction of a wave as it crosses the boundary between two different substances at an angle to the normal. A ray diagram shows it as the incident ray and the refracted ray making different angles with the normal.

concepts.term: Variation of these effects with wavelength
concepts.def: How a substance behaves towards electromagnetic waves is not a single fixed property of that substance. The same substance may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves of different wavelengths in different ways: glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet reaching it, and brick transmits radio waves but not visible light.

concepts.term: Difference in velocity as the cause of refraction
concepts.def: Electromagnetic waves travel at different velocities in different substances. Some effects, refraction among them, are due to that difference in velocity: if the velocity of the wave is the same in both substances, no refraction occurs at the boundary between them.

A construction line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the point where the ray meets it, shown as a dashed line in a ray diagram. Every angle in a ray diagram is measured between a ray and the normal, never between a ray and the boundary.

concepts.term: Angle of incidence and angle of refraction
concepts.def: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of refraction is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal on the far side of the boundary.

A straight line with an arrow on it showing the direction in which the wave is travelling. A ray diagram of refraction shows the incident ray up to the boundary, the normal at that point, and the refracted ray continuing into the second medium.

Draw the boundary, then the normal as a dashed line where the incident ray meets it. A ray passing from air into glass or water bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence. A ray passing from glass or water into air bends away from the normal. A ray that travels along the normal is not bent and carries straight on.

A line joining points on a wave that are all at the same point in their cycle, for example a line along a crest. Wave fronts are drawn at right angles to the direction in which the wave is travelling, and the distance between one wave front and the next is one wavelength.

When a wave front reaches the boundary at an angle, the end that crosses first changes speed first while the rest of the front is still travelling at the original speed. The front is therefore turned, and the direction of travel of the wave changes. In the medium in which the wave travels more slowly the wave fronts are drawn closer together, because the wave moves a shorter distance in each cycle; the frequency of the wave is unchanged.

concepts.term: Dependence of infrared absorption and emission on the surface
concepts.def: Every surface both absorbs and emits infrared radiation, but the amount depends on the nature of the surface. Matt, dark surfaces are the best absorbers and the best emitters of infrared radiation. Shiny, light-coloured surfaces are the poorest absorbers and the poorest emitters, and the best reflectors.

A sealed metal cube whose vertical faces carry different surfaces, typically matt black, matt white, shiny black and shiny silver. It is filled with hot water so that all four faces are at the same temperature, and an infrared detector held the same distance from each face in turn compares the radiation each surface emits.

concepts.term: Control variables in required practical activity 10
concepts.def: Only the nature of the surface may be changed. The distance between the surface and the detector or heater, the time for which readings are taken, the starting temperature, and the position and height of the detector must all be kept the same, or a difference in the readings cannot be attributed to the surface.

AT 1 covers the use of appropriate apparatus to make and record a range of measurements accurately. In this activity that means measuring distance with a ruler, time with a stopwatch, and temperature with a thermometer or infrared detector, and recording those readings to the resolution the instrument allows.

AT 4 covers making observations of the effects of the interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter. In this activity that means observing how infrared radiation interacts with surfaces of different nature — how much each surface absorbs when it faces a radiant heater, and how much each emits when it is hot.

concepts.term: WS and MS opportunities in this practical
concepts.def: The activity also gives opportunities to develop working scientifically skills, such as identifying control variables, judging the resolution and repeatability of measurements and evaluating the method, and mathematical skills, such as tabulating readings, calculating means and plotting temperature against time. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

mcqs.q: A sheet of glass transmits almost all of the visible light that reaches it, but absorbs much of the ultraviolet. What does this show?
options: A material that looks clear must transmit every electromagnetic wave that reaches it.
Whether a substance absorbs or transmits a wave can depend on the wavelength of that wave.
Ultraviolet is absorbed by every substance it meets, whatever that substance is.
Glass reflects the ultraviolet at its surface, so none of it enters the glass at all.
mcqs.explain: Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength, and glass acting differently on two wavelengths is exactly that.

mcqs.q: A mobile phone signal (radio waves) passes through the brick wall of a house, but visible light from outside does not. Which statement explains this best?
options: Brick reflects radio waves back outside, and the phone detects those reflected waves.
Radio waves are absorbed by every material, so brick makes no difference to them.
One substance can transmit one wavelength while absorbing or reflecting another.
A material that stops light must stop all electromagnetic waves reaching it.
mcqs.explain: The behaviour of brick towards electromagnetic waves varies with wavelength: it transmits the long-wavelength radio waves and stops visible light.

mcqs.q: Which statement about substances and electromagnetic waves matches the specification?
options: A given substance treats all wavelengths of electromagnetic wave in the same way.
Absorption is decided by the wave alone, so the substance it meets is irrelevant.
Substances may absorb or reflect electromagnetic waves, but they can never refract them.
Substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves in ways varying with wavelength.
mcqs.explain: This is what the specification states: all four behaviours are possible, and how a substance behaves varies with the wavelength of the wave.

mcqs.q: Refraction of an electromagnetic wave at a boundary between two substances is due to which of the following?
options: The wave bouncing off the boundary between the two substances at an angle.
The difference in the velocity of the wave in the two substances either side of it.
The difference in the frequency of the wave in the two substances either side of it.
The second substance absorbing some of the energy carried by the incoming wave.
mcqs.explain: The specification gives refraction as an example of an effect due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances.

mcqs.q: A wave crosses at an angle into a second substance in which it travels at exactly the same velocity as in the first. What happens at the boundary?
options: It bends towards the normal, because a ray entering any new substance bends that way.
It carries on in the same direction, as there is no difference in velocity to refract it.
It bends away from the normal, because the second substance is a different material.
It is reflected at the boundary, since the wave cannot pass into a new material.
mcqs.explain: Refraction is due to the difference in velocity of the wave in the two substances. With equal velocities that cause is absent, so the direction is unchanged.

mcqs.q: A ray of light travels through air and meets a glass block at an angle of incidence of 40°. In a correct ray diagram, the refracted ray inside the glass is drawn:
options: bent away from the normal, at an angle of refraction larger than 40° from the normal.
bent towards the normal, at an angle of refraction measured as 40° from the boundary.
straight on through the block, since the ray meets a flat boundary between two media.
bent towards the normal, at an angle of refraction smaller than 40° from the normal.
mcqs.explain: A ray passing from air into glass bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is less than the angle of incidence.

mcqs.q: A ray of light inside a glass block reaches the far surface at an angle of incidence of 25° and passes out into the air. In the ray diagram the emerging ray is:
options: bent away from the normal, so the angle from the normal is greater than 25°.
bent towards the normal, because refraction always turns a ray towards the normal.
bent away from the boundary, so the angle from the boundary is greater than 25°.
unchanged in direction, because the ray is leaving the block rather than entering it.
mcqs.explain: A ray passing from glass into air bends away from the normal, so the angle of refraction exceeds the angle of incidence.

mcqs.q: A ray of light travelling through air meets the flat surface of a water tank along the normal. How should the ray diagram be drawn?
options: The ray is drawn bending slightly towards the normal as it enters the water.
The ray is drawn bending away from the normal as it enters the water.
The ray is drawn continuing straight on into the water without changing direction.
The ray is drawn reflected back along its own path into the air.
mcqs.explain: At an angle of incidence of zero there is no change of direction, so the ray is drawn as a straight line through the boundary.

mcqs.q: Which line must be added to a refraction ray diagram before the angles of incidence and refraction can be marked on it?
options: A dashed line at right angles to the boundary where the incident ray meets it.
A dashed line along the boundary itself, from which both angles are measured.
A dashed line at right angles to the incident ray at the point it meets the boundary.
A dashed line continuing the incident ray onwards into the second medium.
mcqs.explain: This is the normal, and both the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction are measured from it.

mcqs.q: A wave front diagram shows water waves crossing at an angle into a region where they travel more slowly. Why does the direction of travel change?
options: The frequency of the wave falls in the new region, which turns each wave front round.
The end of each wave front that crosses first slows first, so the front is turned round.
The wave fronts point along the direction of travel and are dragged round by the boundary.
The wave fronts are reflected at the boundary and then re-enter the slower region.
mcqs.explain: One end of the front changes speed while the other is still travelling faster, which swings the front and so turns the direction of travel.

mcqs.q: In a wave front diagram, a wave passes from a medium where it travels quickly into one where it travels slowly. The wave fronts in the slower medium are drawn:
options: closer together than before, because the wave travels less far in each cycle.
further apart than before, because the wave takes longer to complete each cycle.
closer together than before, because the frequency of the wave has been reduced.
at the same spacing as before, because the wavelength cannot change at a boundary.
mcqs.explain: The frequency is unchanged and the speed is lower, so each cycle covers a shorter distance: the wavelength, which is the spacing of the fronts, is smaller.

mcqs.q: A Leslie cube is filled with hot water and an infrared detector is held the same distance from each face in turn. Which face gives the highest reading?
options: The matt black face, because good absorbers of infrared are also good emitters.
The shiny silver face, because it releases the radiation instead of holding onto it.
Every face reads the same, because the colour of a surface only affects visible light.
The matt white face, because pale surfaces give out the most heat when they are hot.
mcqs.explain: The nature of the surface governs both absorption and emission, and a matt black surface is the best at each.

mcqs.q: Two identical metal plates, one matt black and one shiny silver, are placed the same distance from a radiant heater for ten minutes. What is found?
options: The shiny silver plate rises to the higher temperature, as it holds in more infrared.
Both plates rise to the same temperature, as the surface finish affects only light.
Both plates rise to the same temperature, as they are made of the same metal.
The matt black plate rises to the higher temperature, as it absorbs more infrared.
mcqs.explain: A matt dark surface is the best absorber of infrared radiation, so it gains energy fastest and reaches the higher temperature.

mcqs.q: A student compares the faces of a Leslie cube but holds the detector 5 cm from one face and 15 cm from the next. Why are the results not valid?
options: The detector gives readings in the wrong units when it is moved between the faces.
The water cools during the experiment, which is the only variable that has changed.
Distance has changed as well as the surface, so the difference cannot be attributed to the surface.
Distance from the face makes no difference to the reading, so the test proves nothing.
mcqs.explain: The reading falls as the detector is moved away, so with two variables changing at once the effect of the surface cannot be isolated.
